utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: We recorded that information as reported by families. Now, if we're in a situation where there are two families -- members giving us information simultaneously and it's different, then our staff would probably point out the fact that there's an inconsistency and try to resolve that with them. But, in fact, no, we don't -- we don't conduct investigations to verify this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one follow-up question. Looking at this page, I see that I think four or five times the date of disappearance is recorded of the 1st of January of a year, whether that's 1992 or 1993. Is there any such habit, as I experienced in my work, that sometimes if the exact date of an event is unknown, that it is recorded as the 1st of January of that year? Is that something that you experienced? And, again, I'm quite -- I try to be very transparent. I had that in all kind of different cases, not specifically in DNA cases, but wherever dates of -- which were unknown were often put at the 1st of January of a year. Is that something that you experienced as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the date, the 1st of January of certain year, would give you suspicion that it may not be the accurate date of the event that is described? Is that -- I'm talking about suspicion, not to say it's inaccurate but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with your general experience that a preponderance of such recording would suggest to me that the witness had little more information than the fact that that individual went missing in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock. I think it's time for a break. And when we come back, I think I'll wind it up in the next ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take that break first. Mr. Parsons, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has considered your request that Sasa Lukic be approved to examine the witness Simo -- I don't think that the name is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tusevljak, yes. It's spelled a bit differently on the transcript. That he would examine the witness in-chief and the Chamber grants permission for Sasa Lukic to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to have P7437 again. I would like to remind everyone that it is under seal. I'd like to see page 3, please. Page 3. Thank you. I think we can read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to ask you to explain another entry. It is the 16th registered case from the top. Let's focus on the central right part of the table where it reads that the mortal remains of the person -- apparently the person disappeared on the 18th of August, 1993, in Sanski Most. That's right. Perhaps focus on that part. So Sanski Most. Have you managed to find it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My first question is this: Bearing in mind your last answer concerning the date of entry, in terms of disappearance, that is, we have a precise date here: The 18th of August, 1993. You, as an ICMP director, do you have any specific knowledge of people being buried in the Tomasica grave after the 18th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next question then: The town of Sanski Most, does it tell you anything in terms of any information you may have encountered in the course of your work of people being buried there from Srebrenica or Sanski Most, as the towns designated here as the place of disappearance of certain people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: We've already addressed the fact that this is simply information that we recorded from a family member, and I'm here to testify as an expert with regard to the science that is being presented to the Court. You're asking me to speculate about vague name associations of a town with burials in Srebrenica. I really don't understand what you want me to respond to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you earlier elicited evidence from this witness in which it was clearly outlined what one could learn from DNA testing and what one could not learn. It's even where I asked the Prosecution whether there was any disagreement on that, such as places or cause of death or -- and the witness clearly said and all parties agreed that that's not something you could learn from DNA testing. I even added to it that it seemed pretty obvious. Now you're asking all kind of questions which apparently ignore what the witness said. Unless, Mr. Parsons, you would disagree with this observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you these questions given your position of ICMP director. In this sense, I would also like to ask you the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first of all, don't comment on my ruling. Second, carefully consider your next question, whether you're not doing the same as I earlier said you should refrain from doing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, do you know if in the area of Doboj municipality, in terms of storing the samples taken for DNA analysis, there were situations in which some samples were destroyed before any analysis of those was made?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a need in certain cases to re-exhume the mortal remains previously buried for another sampling that could be used for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't have the details with regard to the cases in question on this list, but that is something that is conducted with some frequency throughout our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court document 1D1123, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is the statement of the person who, at the time of giving the statement, was the head of the federal commission for tracing missing persons. He provided the statement to an OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us focus on page 8 in the B/C/S, paragraph 33, and page 6 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement provided to the OTP investigator, the witness, inter alia, said the following. As the head of the federal commission for tracing missing persons, he knew that in the area of Prijedor there were re-exhumations taking place due to mistakes in the identification process. He goes on to say: "They were buried as unidentified three or four years ago, but, firstly, the DNA samples that were taken before reburial were destroyed due to improper storage; and, secondly, the classical ID method was not done in a proper way." As an ICMP director, did you have information concerning situations such as this one?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, your English phrasing -- the English phrasing that I received in your last sentence permits me to answer in a literal terms, is that I am -- that situations such as those alleged here - I have no information about these particular allegations of Mr. Odobasic - do occur in the course of our work in the Western Balkans. There were many efforts undertaken at many points in the post-war era to identify individuals. Many of those involved traditional identifications by any number of people to include family members themselves identifying who they think are their family members and burying them. And in the course of our work, it -- previous misidentifications, mis-associations, come up when we apply the exact and very strong evidence of DNA science that indicate that -- that checking of previous work may need to be done and that past errors may have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is Ms. Eva Klonowski an ICMP employee?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: She had been for some number of years up until just about the point that I joined the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question to one of the previous questions. The previous question was: "Did you have information concerning situations such as this one," which is a pretty vague question. Now, one of the elements included was that due to improper storage, that samples were destroyed. Are you familiar with that situation as well? I'm asking you this also in view of one of the previous answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to search my memory for those kind of circumstances. No, I can't think of any other situations where that would have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, for that reason, it's always good not to put everything in one bunch together and -- but rather take matters one by one. And, further, you are -- it's implicit more or less in your question that this has directly to do with ICMP storage, for example. Is that clear from the statement? And would you perhaps sit together with Mr. McCloskey and find out to what extent the implicit suggestion that criticism here is expressed on the work of the ICMP, whether that is accurate or not. Because the witness was read only one line of -- one paragraph of a statement without the context. For the time being, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Your Honour. I'll sit down with Mr. McCloskey and deal with these issues. With your leave, can we have another page in this document, the page being number 5 in the English and 7 in the B/C/S; paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The same official of the Federal Commission for Missing Persons Institute in his statement provided to the OTP goes on to say as follows: "One of the bigger mistakes during the Bosanska Krajina exhumations was that the ICMP handed over the Sejkovaca hall with 1.000 bodies to one incompetent physician who had never worked on such jobs. This was Eva Klonowski's assistant, Nermin Sarajlic. He never carried out a single independent autopsy or exhumation." During your tenure with the ICMP, did a physician by the name of Nermin Sarajlic work for the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Nermin Sarajlic worked at the KIP facility in Sanski Most as an ICMP employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what were his tasks.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know the breadth of his task but he was involved in mortuary management, examination of the bodies and sampling for DNA testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have any experience with the physician, would it tend to confirm the opinion of the head of the Federal Commission for Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you one follow-up question, which I would have expected before the last one. Was the -- performing autopsies or doing exhumations, was that part of the job of Nermin Sarajlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My belief is that Nermin is a forensic pathologist with also training in anthropology, so he would be more engaged in the mortuary examination of the remains as opposed to the exhumation and recovery, if my knowledge is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you expect autopsy to be part of what you described as mortuary examination of the remains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then perhaps one more question. Do you have any knowledge about whether he ever did an independent autopsy or whether he never did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there's an issue of some timing here. I don't know when this -- these statements were made in relation to Dr. Sarajlic's experience. But, generally speaking, I would think that that is not a true statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the statement was taken, Mr. Stojanovic, if you would permit me, in 2005. Does that in any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm -- I don't want to go beyond my knowledge. It would surprise me greatly if that were true in 2005 but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would suffice or surprise you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would surprise me if this statement were correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if experts wishing to assist the Defence had the need to carry out analysis of the report created by the ICMP with regard to matching and identification and the number of bodies, would they be able to access all necessary evidence material for them to be able to perform such a task today?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: You make reference to the report, and the answer theoretically is yes, that evidence exists. Would they be able to perform such a task would depend on agreements that were made. So we have some context here to answer that question. In the trial of Radovan Karadzic, a great deal of issue was made with regard to access to the DNA data and the scientific underpinnings of the DNA match reports of the ICMP, and we worked extensively with Defence and the Office of the Prosecutor to designate a representative sampling of DNA match reports representing different periods of time, different geographical regions, et cetera, to permit Defence to have reviewed those DNA case files. It's of critical importance in this aspect that these were only turned over to Defence under very narrow and negotiated conditions and, moreover, only with consent of all family members involved in the DNA match reports. The last part is very crucial, and so we went to vast amounts of effort to reach out to family members to ask them if they would be willing for their genetic and personal information to be released to the Court to permit Defence counter-examination, and we were very successful in obtaining a representative sampling of that -- of case files that were submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. At this point, we have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. McCloskey, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, the Judges have no further questions for you either, which means that this concludes your evidence in this court. I may have said the same last time when you were here, and then it turned out not to be true because it did not conclude the evidence. Nevertheless, I wish you a safe return home again, and thank you very much for coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- no speaking aloud. Mr. Stojanovic and/or Mr. Ivetic, I think we could now continue to hear the testimony and cross-examination of Mr. Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's our understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- I see the usher has left the courtroom so I don't know what initiative ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and if I could be excused, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, not having reviewed the time sheets, is it a fair assumption that you would need at least the rest of this day?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And probably some -- I think it was 15 or 20 minutes tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's mainly for the next witness, that there's no need to have the next witness to remain on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the next witness was actually already excused based upon my conversations with the Prosecution previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then there's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, at the beginning of your testimony, you gave a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That solemn declaration is still binding upon you. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we left off talking about your first report, P7434 MFI, and we were at page 102 in the English and page 64 in the B/C/S, which we could call up just to refresh everyone's recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Just to say we've got the colour copies of Mr. Franjic's report so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- perhaps it might make sense to give them out to him. With the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you need to inspect them --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, we did that last -- last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I trust them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness can be given the ... you may directly give it to the witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as you recall, sir, we left off talking about the lack of any comparison photographs or photomicrographs in your report for the part dealing with your conclusions from your analysis. The question I want to start with today is: Do you believe that your practice of not including photographs or photomicrographs of positive matches is in compliance with industry standards for this type of review as would be undertaken by other AFTE members?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on a case-to-case basis. Members of the AFTE sometimes do not include photographs of matches, as you put it, in their reports or comparisons of microscopic traces of ejectors with traces of the firing pin and so on. It all depends on the policy of the laboratory which has asked for this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is the policy of the laboratory that you operate under for other cases apart from the Tomasica investigation? Do you provide photographic or photomicrographic comparisons of matches that have been determined?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on the expert who is doing the expert analysis. As I stated here, individual characteristics have been explained by comparison of cartridges. As I say, there are seven cartridges of 7.62 millimetre by 39 millimetre characteristics. Joint and individual characteristics have been established and then I list the individual characteristics. The micro ridges, the traces of the breech face and so on. There are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down because the interpreters have difficulties in following you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. So I have described that in addition to common characteristics which are manifested as common micro ridges, that is to say, the common form and position of the traces of the firing pin, the breech face, the ejector, the extractor, and the case cover, that common individual characteristics were also established which are manifested in the form of common micro ridges within the traces of the ejector, the breech face, and the case cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, your answer has dealt with the characteristics of a cartridge. Taking into account both cartridges and bullets, are you in a position to state what methodology and process was used by you, such as the minimum number of matching general individual characteristics or marks when compared with a known fired sample before reaching a determination of a match?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A comparison was made here of seven. Let's take these seven as an example. Seven disputed cartridges, bullets of 7.62 by 39 millimetre calibre, 8B, 9B, 36B, 38B, 42B, and from body number TOM-04-PRD-302T and from the body --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you. We see all that in your report. What I'm asking is what's not in your report. What was the minimum number of matching general individual or other characteristics that was necessary in your comparison for you to conclude that either two cartridges matched or two spent bullets matched?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By contrast with identification of bullet and fragments of bullets which is made on the basis of common individual characteristics, such as common micro ridges, grooves, lands and grooves and their traces, where we can talk about the number of possible individual characteristics, identification of cartridges fired from a fire-arm is done based on common general and individual characteristics. So we then have also the trace of the firing pin and the trace of the breech face, the trace of the ejector, the trace of the extractor, the trace of the case cover, the trace of the bedding of the bullet, the trace of the clip. There are therefore several traces on the basis of which both general and individual identification is made. In the finding, common individual characteristics were established within the traces of the ejector, the breech face, and the case cover in the form of micro-rough surfaces, so it can be concluded with certainty that they were fired from one and the same fire-arm. As I stated previously, in addition to the expert report of the 7th of May, 2014, enclosed are all the cases that were analysed during the expert analysis, including the 18 disputed cartridges, so that what we are talking about now can be checked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, your report has been submitted to us as evidence, and I'm asking about your report. Where can we find in your report the number of characteristics that were matched for each of the cartridges and each of the bullets that you matched and said were fired from an either similar type of gun or similar gun?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no number here. The number of traces, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in a proofing note we received from the Prosecution on the 23rd of June, 2015, we, for the first time, learned that you not only manually examined bullets but that you also utilised a computer database as a way to ensure that no potential matches were missed. First of all, can you tell us why that information about the use of a computer database is not contained in your reports?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 5 of the written report on the analysis, in the section ballistics forensic analysis, the first paragraph says: "The analysis was conducted by visually examining, measuring, weighing, using a Nikon SMZ1000 and Olympus SZX12 stereo microscope, then Leica FS C and Zrak MK-1 comparative microscopes, and by using various databases, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This can be found in the English version on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree with me that neither the Nikon SMZ1000, nor the Olympus microscope, nor the Leica, nor Zrak MK-1 refer to a computer?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the identification of what computer software and system you used is essential to determining the reliability of any comparisons made by a computer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get things straight. Witness, before you answer that question, when you said that you used various databases, were these databases just hard copies or were they stored in any computer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both hard copies and on computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you referred to having used computer databases, did you refer to the same or to different databases as you mentioned in your report? In your -- in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By using various databases, including both those in hard copy and softwares. That is to say, computer databases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How -- how did you use those computer databases? Did you -- was the -- were these programmes used for seeking matches based on that software, or did you consult those databases for the main characteristics of the cases and the bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were primarily used in order to establish whether the disputed cartridges were fired from one fire-arm or from multiple fire-arms. That was why comparative microscope was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not, at this moment, talking about the use of microscope. My question is focused on how did you use those databases? Were those databases used as reference materials, or was it used in order to -- computerised comparison?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honour. It might help to ask if it was automated or not. That might be a quicker way of getting to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. Whether it was automatised through this software, automatised identification, or did you use those databases as reference materials such as then providing measurements, numbers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No automatised search of cartridges and rounds such as the IBIS system and others was used. No automatised systems, but data such as general rifling characteristics, where information is to be found for more than 20.000 different sorts of fire-arms of various calibres. It includes data on -- as for rounds, calibre, the number of lands and grooves, the direction and spiralling angle of the traces of lands and grooves, the width of lands and grooves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question. Perhaps there was more in those databases but this is the type of information you found there. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the report that we have in front of us, and let's talk -- let's first deal with the seven disputed 7.69 by 39 millimetre cartridges that you concluded came from the same fire-arm but you could not determine if they came --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, you mean 7.62.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. 7.62. And you determined that they came from Kalashnikov rifle -- pardon me. They could have come from a Kalashnikov rifle, an M70 rifle, or an M72 rifle machine-gun. Is it because all three of these classes of fire-arms have similar general characteristics in terms of the breech firing pin and the ejector, the reason why you could not further narrow the potential source of those fired cartridges?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. They all have common general characteristics. The position and the pattern of the trace of firing pin, the trace of the breech face, the extractor, ejector, and the trace of the indication cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 21 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, I believe you detail the review of these cartridges and you say that you microscopically reviewed them against undisputed cartridges fired from an M70 and an M72. First of all, did you or someone else test fire and recover known sample cartridges for these two weapons or did you use some sort of computer or other database for your known sample?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Centre for Forensic and Information Support of the Federal Police Administration in the Section for Ballistics and Mechanoscopic Analysis, there are collections of undisputed cartridges and undisputed rounds which were received during test firings from fire-arms, which is the subject of expert analysis, so that this collection contains hundreds of thousands of cartridges and rounds originating from bullets fired from automatic rifles of the Kalashnikov type and also M70 and M72 machine-gun and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that you mentioned the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm glad that you mentioned the Kalashnikov. Your conclusion could not exclude -- also link the Kalashnikov as a possible source for this -- for these cartridges, but nowhere in your report do I see that you reviewed microscopically a known Kalashnikov bullet or cartridge with these in order to reach such a determination. Did you, in fact, review with a known sample of a test-fired Kalashnikov cartridge?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the last 18 years, as long as I've been working on ballistic forensic analysis, I examined thousands of undisputed cartridges fired from Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think you're perhaps missing the gist of the question. In your report, you say that you compared 37B, 44B, 45B, 47B, 49B, and 56B with undisputed cartridges of bullets fired from the Crvena Zastava rifle. The question I think Mr. Ivetic is a seeking an answer for is: Did you also compare these cartridges with undisputed cartridges of other arms, such as arms of the Kalashnikov type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think that was primarily your question, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then the other part of that was: Why is that not listed in this section of the report, which particular type of Kalashnikov weapon whose spent cartridge from a known sample you reviewed, since there is an entire family of Kalashnikovs with various characteristics?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All cartridges of bullets of the 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre, as I already stated, have common general characteristics, including Kalashnikov, AK-47, AKM, the AKMS model, of various manufacturers, be they Russian produced or Romanian, Bulgarian, East Germany produced, and others. Therefore, it was not necessary to compare undisputed cartridges with undisputed cartridges. So all these cartridges of the 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre have identical general characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you therefore then agree that in order to link two cartridges as being fired from the same type of fire-arm, we would need to look at individual characteristics rather than these general class characteristics; and in doing so, it is customary to identify, by way of comparison photograph or number of minimum matching marks, those which these specific cartridges have in common which other cartridges fired from similar guns of the same calibre would not have?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are mistaken. You're mixing up the comparison of general versus individual characteristics. In my report, I stated that the mutual comparison, for example, of seven cartridges of 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre, in addition to common general characteristics, also common individual characteristics were found. Comparing the seven cartridges with undisputed cartridges resulted in some general common general characteristics being established. There were no individual characteristics involved as well as their number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to -- before we take the break. Witness, what Mr. Ivetic apparently wants to know is if you compared the six disputed cartridges with the Crvena Zastava, and if you compared them with other types of weapons as well, including Kalashnikov, why did you only report that the common characteristics matched the common characteristics of the Crvena Zastava and why didn't you say anything about the outcome of the other comparisons you have made with other types of weapons, including Kalashnikovs? That's the question, I think, Mr. Ivetic. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the six cartridges you just mentioned, 37B, 44B, 47B, 49B, and 56B, in addition to common general characteristics, some common individual characteristics were found as well. On that basis, it can be concluded that they were fired from one and the same fire-arm. And then in the paragraph on page 14 of the expert analysis, it is stated that by detailed microscopic examination and by comparison of these six disputed cartridges with undisputed cartridges originating from bullets fired from semi-automatic rather than automatic rifle of Crvena Zastava make, M57/66, common general characteristics were found which manifest themselves as common shape and mutual position of imprints of traces of the ejector, cartridge extractor, the firing pin, and the face. In the opinion, which can be found on page 64 of the expert analysis, it is stated that the six disputed cartridges of 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre, marked as 37B, 44B, 45B, 47B, 49B, and 56B, originate from bullets fired from one and the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. I think, perhaps, Mr. Ivetic, but certainly myself, do not understand that if those six cartridges were fired by the same fire-arm on the basis of individual characteristics found on those cartridges, why that necessarily is from a Crvena Zastava rifle rather than, for example, a Kalashnikov, all six cartridges fired by that Kalashnikov, which, if I understand you well, has the same general characteristics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they do not have common general characteristics as the cartridges of 7.62 by 39-millimetre calibre rounds or bullets as the cartridges fired from Kalashnikov automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- we take a break first, and then I leave it in your hands, Mr. Ivetic, to finally clarify the issue which apparently puzzles you and puzzles me to some extent as well. We take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, and that will be quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I will try to go step by step to clear up the matter that was first raised by Judge Orie's questions to you. Before I do that, sir, would you agree with us, with me at least, that explaining to the Judges and to I [sic] and to another expert would be much easier if you had comparison photographs or photomicrographs contained in your report clearly identifying those marks which you relied upon to confirm a match?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to 1D5461 in e-court. 1D5461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see the message on the screen, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do and I have it open on my e-court on the other screen, so I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can also see it on my e-court screen, so it might be a court-related problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he says it is open on his screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As counsel said, it is opening on his as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think maybe they're our personal e-court screens rather the court's e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be that there is some kind of release necessary to get it us to as well, instead of having it available for the parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I thought if it was released to the Prosecution and -- that the Court are the same entity, but let me see if I can try and find an alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Registrar could assist that would be -- there we are. We have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a brochure that I found on the web site of the Unis Igman d.d. company. Would you agree that this is the same company that you referred to in your report as Igman Konjic as the manufacturer of the 7.62 by 39-millimetre cartridges that we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But the year of production is different. Or other years of production. These are newer bullets whereas the cartridges date back to the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And right now we're talking about the cartridges. I'd like to turn to page 2 which should related to the M67 ball, which I believe is a type of bullet you talked about in your report. And here, according to the manufacturer, we see that this cartridge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first seek verification of your assumption, Mr. Ivetic. You said you believe "this is a type of bullet you talked about in your report." Is this the type of bullet or even the bullet you talked about in your report, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. It is a bullet of 7.62 by 39-millimetres calibre, and its round is M67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, earlier you made a comment about the year of production. Is -- where -- was this projectile, was this produced in the same years as the projectiles you examined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The projectiles I examined are such that one cannot establish year of production. Year of production can only be ascertained according to the markings made on the bottom of the 18 cartridges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know whether we can see here what is on the bottom or not. But please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can try to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in your analysis you identified certain cartridges with the Cyrillic letters I and K and concluded that they came from Igman Konjic of various years of manufacture from 1976 to approximately 1983 in your first report? Is that a fair rendition of what you contain in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not INK, but IK. The Cyrillic designation was IK.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the cartridges had the IK inscription in Cyrillic except for one. In Latinic script, it said PKI 1894 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in looking at what is reported in this brochure as the use for this round, we see the semi-automatic rifle M59/66, the automatic rifle M70, the light machine-gun M72, and weapons 7.62 Kalashnikov AK-47 SKS and RPK. Would you agree with this publication that this particular cartridge when attached with this particular bullet can be fired from all of the weapons that are listed here that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I think to clarify the point where you and Judge Orie had confusion, I believe you were earlier saying that the M59 semi-automatic rifle, M59/66, can be distinguished from automatic rifles firing the same round because of different ejector marks. Am I generally speaking correct about what you were trying to explain before the break?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no confusion in my mind whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, again, I do not understand your question. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try again, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we're both trying to fully understand the evidence of this witness. Did you tell us that the markings left on this projectile, when fired by an M59/66 are different from the markings left on this projectile, and that is bullet together with cartridge, when fired by an M70 and M72 or the Kalashnikov AK-47 SKS or RPK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no difference in terms of markings on the rounds and projectiles fired from a semi-automatic rifle, M59/66, and rounds fired from automatic rifles M70, a light machine-gun, M72, and the automatic rifles Kalashnikov. So one cannot identify which weapon was used to fire it because they share the same common general characteristics, but only when we discuss markings or traces on the rounds as opposed to the cartridges fired from those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say on the cartridge, you cannot distinguish whether it was fired by any of those weapons; but if you have the round itself, then you can distinguish which type of weapon was used, which of those four was used when firing that round? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the other way around. In terms of bullets it cannot be done; in terms of cartridges it can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's now clarified. So if you see such a cartridge, you could know whether it was fired by an M59/66 or by any of the other weapons mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I leave it further in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one question before this we go on to another area. Now relation to the automatic weapons chambered for 7.62 by 39-millimetre round, you cannot tell if those cartridges were fired from a Crvena Zastava Kalashnikov-type rifle or a Kalashnikov-type rifle manufactured by someone else, such as a Chinese-type 56 or the Czech VZ-58, can you?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, it cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we -- if this is in e-court now, can we ask for it to be tendered as a -- perhaps even -- perhaps MFI'd if it's not, so we can sort out what pages are in e-court, if we need all of them, et cetera. It's about a four-page document but I'm only really concerned about the first page which shows the source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll reserve a number. You'll decide what pages you need. The Prosecution has an opportunity to add anything. And then we'll decide on admission once it has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be reserved would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be D1085, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1085 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at 1D5466.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number, as I said before, is reserved for this exhibit still to be further defined and uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you repeat the number again? It doesn't look like the same on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 1D5466.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a publication entitled: A survey of image processing techniques and statistics for ballistic specimens in forensic science. And it's from the Science & Justice journal, January 2012. I would like to look at page 5 together. And, first of all, if we look at the figure in the upper right-hand part of the page we see a diagram of a microscope. Does Figure 5 comport to the set-up that is typically used to perform the analysis and comparison of known to unknown cartridges as well as bullet rounds, with a camera mounted on the top of the microscope, then an eye piece, then an optical bridge connecting two sets of objective lenses, and then the stage holding the sample on the one side and the disputed on the other?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the type of set-up that you used in your laboratory performing this analysis?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I noted that both this document but also the previous one apparently have no English -- no B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now there are two issues. First of all, whether the Defence can live with a -- the absence of any B/C/S version but also whether the public can live with it. Because it's the -- the public character of this -- of this trial has both an internal and an external aspect. The internal aspect apparently seems to be no problem for you, but the external aspect, of course, is a bit different. The public can't follow what is said here. So if you would please also look at that when further --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And I think you'll see that the ones that I'm using now are more pictures and I will read any text that I'm relying upon. But definitely with ones that are more substantive in nature we will want to have a translation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it mainly about the pictures, then, of course, it's less of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could turn to the next page in this document and look at figure number 6 on the page at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have been talking about comparison photomicrographs. The top, I believe, are two such images: The one on the left of a round that has been fired and the one on the right of the cartridge that has been fired. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because on the left-hand side, we have a comparative photograph of two rounds, and on the right-hand side, a comparative photograph of two cartridges. So not one but two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And earlier you said you had taken photographs for purposes of the analysis did you in Tomasica. Did you take photographs and preserve photographs of this nature comparing two cartridges or two rounds in a photograph or photomicrograph?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was compared but it wasn't photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn back to the prior page, I'd like to focus on the right-hand column and the second full paragraph on the right-hand column, the third paragraph in total, and I'll read it to you so you get a translation. It says as follows: "As this paper is principally concerned with the identification of striae, identification of two bullets to a common source will be used as a first example. As the two bullets are aligned, the investigator looks for how well the striae are lined and the similarity in their width and amplitude. The test is considered a match if two fire-arm examiners concur that it is a match, as specified in the Association of Fire-arm and Tool Mark Examiners Theory of Identification." And that's the end of the citation. Sir, do you agree with this publication that the identification method as prescribed by the AFTE requires two fire-arm examiners to agree on a match after looking at the comparison before determining a match has been made?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you quoted here refers to rounds, so the striae or the grooves are the traces on rounds within the traces of lands and grooves. In my report, I did not mention the striae but only the traces of lands and grooves which are appropriate for a general identification, but they are inappropriate for mutual comparison. As for -- or, rather, by contrast to traces on rounds, there are traces on cartridges here. The traces of the firing pin, the breech face, the ejector, the case cover, not the striae. In the findings, both I and my colleague, expert witness Alija Kotarevic, looked at cartridges, so first I and then he after me, and we came to a joint opinion which is provided in the findings of our expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I agree as to the first report. But would you agree with me the second report, which we looked at last week, and I believe you even testified at transcript page 36403 that did you that report all by yourself, and yet that report also looked at cartridges in addition to rounds being analysed, would you agree the second report did not have a second forensic examiner looking at the comparisons that you saw and made?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO FRANJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. However, by contrast with the first report, where 18 disputed cartridges were examined and their calibre was 7.62 by 39 millimetres, in the second report, there was just one cartridge of the 7.62 by 39 calibre and one cartridge of the 7.9 by 59 millimetres. So that this one cartridges of the 7.62 by 39-millimetres' calibre -- I'm sorry, but there is an error in the transcript. It should be 7.9 by 59 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It now says 59, but in the English version of your second report, Witness, I think at the very bottom on e-court page 50 it says: 7.9 by 57 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by 57. It should read: By 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're at the time where we should not proceed, as a matter of fact. Witness, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, and meanwhile I instruct you again that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 30th of June, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of June, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
